Lowest epoch first, because an attestation targets the current or previous epoch, so an older target is the least likely to be read again. Inserts with their eviction pass, and justified promotion in `updateCheckpoints`, take a new mutex, `checkpointStatesMu`, so that concurrent misses cannot leave more than ten entries and each eviction pass sees a stable justified checkpoint. A checkpoint evicted before it becomes justified is built again by the next read. Lookups do not take the new mutex, and `getCheckpointState` still does not take `f.mu`. Finalization pruning is unchanged.

## Not changed here

- `OnAttestation` still builds a missing target checkpoint state while it holds `f.mu`. With the bound, an evicted target is built again there if it is requested again; if more than nine checkpoints other than the justified one are in use at the same time, entries can be rebuilt repeatedly. Building checkpoint states outside `f.mu` is a separate change.
- `newCheckpointState` copies the RANDAO mixes together with their merkle tree when the source state has one, although it reads only one mix, to compute the shuffling. Copying the mixes without the tree would make each entry smaller.
- Concurrent misses for the same checkpoint still build it more than once, as before.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/forkchoice.go`: the `maxCheckpointStates` constant and the `checkpointStatesMu` field.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/utils.go`: `getCheckpointState` stores through the new `storeCheckpointState`, which evicts above the cap; `updateCheckpoints` promotes the justified checkpoint under `checkpointStatesMu`.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/forkchoice_test.go`: five tests.

## Testing

- **TDD:** with `utils.go` from `main` (only the `maxCheckpointStates` constant and the `checkpointStatesMu` field added), all five new tests fail: `TestCheckpointStatesBoundedWithoutFinalization` (11 entries, want 10), `TestCheckpointStatesKeepJustStoredState` (11), `TestCheckpointStatesKeepCurrentJustified` (12), `TestJustifiedPromotionWaitsForCheckpointStateEviction` and `TestCheckpointStateEvictionWaitsForJustifiedPromotion`. Removing one part of the change at a time: `TestCheckpointStatesKeepCurrentJustified`, whose justified checkpoint has the lowest epoch, fails when the justified checkpoint is not excluded from eviction; `TestCheckpointStatesKeepJustStoredState` fails when the entry just stored is not excluded; the two lock tests fail when `updateCheckpoints` or `storeCheckpointState` does not take `checkpointStatesMu`. All five pass with the change.
- `go test -p 2 ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/...`, also with `-race`.
- `fork_choice` spec tests (`go test -run 'Test/mainnet/.*/fork_choice' ./cl/spectest/`): no failures, and the same tests pass and skip as on `main`.
- `make lint`, `make erigon integration`.
author: domiwei

title: cl/phase1/network/services: reject aggregates whose aggregation bits have the wrong length
body:
## Summary

Caplin's `beacon_aggregate_and_proof` validation did not check that the aggregate's `aggregation_bits` length equals the size of the selected committee. The Electra and Gloas gossip specs require `len(aggregation_bits) == len(get_beacon_committee(state, aggregate.data.slot, index))` and reject the aggregate otherwise. Lighthouse and Prysm enforce it.

`ProcessMessage` fetched the committee but only called `GetAttestingIndicies(aggregate, false)`. From Electra on, that accessor ignores the flag and, for this single-committee call, rejects bitlists that are too short but not those that are too long. Before Electra, it performs the exact-length check only when the flag is true. For `aggregation_bits`, `ValidateForConfig` checks only the fork-wide maximum, not the selected committee size. So an aggregate with extra trailing bits, unset or set, passed validation. The aggregate attestation signature was checked against only the in-range committee members, and the selected aggregator signs the whole `AggregateAndProof`, so all BLS checks could pass. Before Electra, a bitlist that is too short could also pass if its bytes still covered the committee.

Trigger: the aggregate must be signed by a validator that is selected as aggregator for that slot, so it comes from a malicious or buggy aggregator; a relaying peer cannot change the bitlist of an honest aggregate.

Impact, on nodes that fully verify gossip aggregates (nodes with local validators; from Fulu on, only nodes with a local proposer in the current or next epoch) and for aggregates submitted through `POST /eth/v1/validator/aggregate_and_proofs`:

- the invalid aggregate was accepted and forwarded; peers that enforce this rule reject it;
- it was added to the attestation pool;
- from Electra on, block production could include it, and the block transition, which requires an exact length, then rejected the locally produced block, so the local proposal failed.

The fix rejects the aggregate when `aggregation_bits` length differs from the committee size, right after the committee is fetched. It applies to all forks because a `beacon_aggregate_and_proof` gossip aggregate selects exactly one committee. The REST endpoint goes through the same `ProcessMessage`, so it is covered too.

## Not changed here

- `GetAttestingIndicies` in `cl/phase1/core/state/cache_accessors.go` still ignores `checkBitsLength` from Electra on (and has no final length check), and `getAttestingIndicies` in `cl/phase1/forkchoice/checkpoint_state.go` also does not reject bitlists that are too long. Enforcing the length there would be defense in depth for the other callers (fork choice, block production); this PR only adds the gossip rule.
- Block production and the attestation pool are not changed: the pool is filled only by this service, so wrong-length aggregates no longer reach it.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/network/services/aggregate_and_proof_service.go`: reject an aggregate whose `aggregation_bits` length differs from the committee size.
- `cl/phase1/network/services/aggregate_and_proof_service_test.go`: two new tests; the two shared fixtures used 9 bits for an 8-member committee and now use 8.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestAggregateAndProofRejectsAggregationBitsLengthMismatch` uses the real Electra fixture under Electra, Fulu and Gloas configs, with `n-1` and `n` bits and with `n+1` bits whose trailing bit is either unset or set. `TestAggregateAndProofRejectsAggregationBitsLengthMismatchBeforeElectra` checks `n-1` bits and `n+1` bits (trailing bit unset or set) under Phase0. With the production file from `main`, only these subtests fail, because `main` accepts these aggregates: the six `n+1` subtests under Electra, Fulu and Gloas, and all three Phase0 subtests. The Electra, Fulu and Gloas `n-1` and `n` cases pass on `main` and with the fix. All other `TestAggregateAndProof*` tests pass on `main` with the fixture change.
- `go test -p 2 -count=1 ./cl/phase1/network/services/ ./cl/beacon/handler/` passed.
- `make lint` reported 0 issues on two runs.
- `make erigon integration` succeeded.
author: domiwei

title: execution, cl: reject block access indices beyond len(transactions)+1
body:
EIP-7928 bounds every `block_access_index` by `len(transactions) + 1`, the post-execution index, but `ValidateForBlock` only knew the block gas limit. A BAL whose indices lie past that bound passed every up-front check and was refuted only after the block had been executed and its computed BAL compared against the header. By then the parallel executor had already expanded each spurious change into version-map cells, so a payload could make a node do a disproportionate amount of work before it answered INVALID.

`ValidateForBlock` now takes the transaction count and rejects an out-of-range index at every entry point that has the block body: `engine_newPayload`, `InsertBlocks`, the Caplin payload path and the block builder. The eth/71 BAL fetcher only knows the header, so it keeps the gas-limit checks under the name `ValidateForHeader`; the blocks it assembles are bounded again by `InsertBlocks`. The sidecar memoizes the two levels separately, so a header-validated BAL only pays the index pass on insert.

`TransactionsSSZ` gains a nil-safe `Len`, since a payload built by `NewEth1Block` has no transaction list.

## Tests

- `execution/types`: `TestBlockAccessListValidateForBlockBoundsIndices` covers all four change lists, accepting `len(transactions) + 1` and rejecting `+ 2`, and checks that `ValidateForHeader` stays index-agnostic. The sidecar memo test also covers a changed transaction count. Both were red before the check existed.
- `engine_newPayloadV5`: an out-of-range index returns INVALID naming the block access index before insertion. With the check stubbed out, the same payload was executed and failed only with "block access list mismatch". The in-range post-execution index is kept as a control.
- `InsertBlocks` and Caplin's `DecodeAndValidateBlockAccessList` get the same pair. The `InsertBlocks` test fails when the bound is disabled.

The behaviour change followed red → green. The `ValidateForHeader` split and the `Len` accessor are mechanical and rely on the existing suites.

Fixes ethereum-bounty/erigon#33
author: yperbasis

title: cl/phase1/forkchoice: fix the anchor checkpoint epoch for a mid-epoch block post-state
body:
## Summary

After a restart, Caplin can send peers a Status whose finalized epoch and root are not a checkpoint of the chain. In a devnet run, a Lighthouse node banned the restarted node for it.

This happened on a Gloas devnet with 32 slots per epoch and Lighthouse, Teku, Prysm, Nimbus and Caplin nodes. An Erigon node with embedded Caplin was restarted at 15:24:03 UTC and resumed from its saved finalized state at slot 95. Block 95 (`0x2e5222cf…`) was the epoch-3 checkpoint block, because slot 96 was empty. At 15:24:04.871 a Lighthouse node received this Status from it: `finalized_epoch: 2`, `finalized_root: 0x2e5222cf…`. Lighthouse logged `Handshake Failure ... reason: "Different finalized chain"`, sent a Goodbye with `Irrelevant Network` and banned the peer (`score: -100.00`). The node's later connection attempts to that Lighthouse node, at 15:54, 16:03, 16:04 and 16:34, failed, and Lighthouse still listed it as banned at 16:44:08, more than 80 minutes later. A second restart began at 16:03:58 and resumed from slot 256, an epoch start; another Lighthouse node accepted its Status at 16:04:01 and still listed it as connected at 16:44:08.

`saveFinalizedStateOnDiskIfNeeded` (`cl/phase1/stages/forkchoice.go`) saves the state that fork choice holds for the finalized checkpoint root, without advancing it to the start slot of the checkpoint epoch. In this run, that state was the post-state of block 95 at slot 95. `NewForkChoiceStore` took the anchor checkpoint epoch from the anchor state's slot, so it set the justified, finalized and unrealized checkpoints to `(2, root of block 95)`. That pair is not a checkpoint of the chain: the epoch-2 boundary, slot 64, is before block 95. The initial Status and the later `SetStatus` calls of the Caplin stages take the finalized epoch from `FinalizedCheckpoint()`. In this handshake, Lighthouse had finalized epoch 4 and compared the peer's `finalized_root` with its own block root at slot 64, the start of the advertised epoch 2. The pair stays until fork choice applies a higher finalized checkpoint from imported blocks; the Lighthouse handshake came within two seconds of the restart, before that. Fork choice used the same pair internally; for example, on the first lookup, `getCheckpointState` used the slot-95 state for epoch 2 without advancing it.

**Trigger:** a restart that resumes from a saved finalized state that is the post-state of a checkpoint block not at an epoch start. This happens when the first slot of the checkpoint's epoch had no block and the last canonical block before that slot is not itself at an epoch start. When remote checkpoint sync is enabled, Caplin uses a readable same-network saved state directly if it is within the resume horizon, or as a fallback if the remote fetch fails; when remote checkpoint sync is disabled, including on a devnet without a custom checkpoint URL, the local syncer uses a valid saved state if one is available. How often this happens depends on the network's missed-slot rate; on this devnet, the canonical chain had no block at 3 of the 18 epoch starts from slot 32 to slot 576 (slots 96, 224 and 512). A remote server that returns the post-state of a finalized checkpoint block that is not at an epoch start would cause the same; in the reviewed Lighthouse, Teku and Prysm code, `states/finalized` returns the state at the start slot of the finalized epoch, but Caplin's own `states/finalized` can return the block's post-state.

**Impact:** in this run, a Lighthouse node rejected the handshake, banned the restarted node and still listed it as banned more than 80 minutes later.

**Fix:** a checkpoint block at a slot that is not an epoch start is the checkpoint of a later epoch. So no canonical block lies between it and the start of the next epoch, and it is also the checkpoint of that epoch: block 95 is the epoch-3 checkpoint because no canonical block lies between it and slot 96. When the anchor state is the post-state of its latest block (its latest block header slot is the state slot) and that slot is not an epoch start, `NewForkChoiceStore` now uses the next epoch: `(3, root of block 95)` in the run above. For this case, a node that finalized epoch 3 without a restart holds the same pair, and so does a node that checkpoint-syncs from a server returning the state advanced to slot 96. Genesis, epoch-aligned states and states advanced past their block keep the epoch of their own slot, as before. The anchor state, its slot and the anchor root are unchanged.

## Not changed here

- The saved file still holds one state and does not store the epoch that fork choice had finalized with that root. When the state is a block post-state and whole epochs after the block were empty, the block is the checkpoint of several epochs, and the store starts from the earliest of them. That can be lower than the finalized epoch, but it is a checkpoint of the chain, and it stays until fork choice applies a higher finalized checkpoint. Restoring the exact epoch would need it to be saved with the state or taken from another durable source.
- `FinalizedSlot()` still returns the last slot of the finalized epoch. After an epoch-start checkpoint anchor, for example from remote checkpoint sync or a restart from an epoch-aligned state, it can include slots after the anchor whose blocks are not imported yet, and the Gloas payload verification sweep in chain-tip sync stops at it. For the slot-95 anchor it moves from 95 to 127, the value that a node checkpoint-synced from the state at slot 96 already gets.
- The initial Status, which later `SetStatus` calls replace, still has `HeadSlot: 0` with the anchor root as `head_root` (`cmd/caplin/caplin1/run.go`).

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/forkchoice.go`: in `NewForkChoiceStore`, the anchor checkpoint epoch is the state's epoch plus one when the anchor state is the post-state of its latest block and its slot is not an epoch start.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/forkchoice_test.go`: new `TestNewForkChoiceStoreAnchorCheckpointEpoch` with three anchors and their expected checkpoint epochs: a state at slot 96 whose latest block is at 95 (epoch 3), the post-state of a block at slot 95 (epoch 3), and a state at slot 95 whose latest block is at 94 (epoch 2).

## Testing

- **TDD:** with the production file from `main` (362e903341f), the slot-95 block post-state case of `TestNewForkChoiceStoreAnchorCheckpointEpoch` fails (finalized and justified epoch 2, want 3); the two other cases pass. All three pass with the change.
- The anchor states of the consensus spec fork_choice and sync tests are all at slot 0 (checked on a local fixture copy, 234 files), so the change does not apply to them.
- `go test -p 2 ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/... ./cl/phase1/stages/...`, `make lint`, `make erigon integration`.
author: domiwei

title: cl/p2p, cmd/utils, docs: follow-ups to the Caplin IP block limits
body:
Follow-up to #24815 (part of #24444): domiwei's review of its last head, which came after the merge.

## Changes

- **IPv6 /48 cap**: `WithLimitPerSubnet` replaces go-libp2p's whole IPv6 list, which caps an IPv6 /48 at 64. Our /48 cap, `max(16, max-peer-count/8)`, was above that from `--caplin.max-peer-count=520` on (128 at 1024), so one /48 could hold more connections than in released versions. The /48 cap is now at most 64. At the default `--caplin.max-peer-count=128` the cap stays 16.
- **Trusted loopback**: a trusted CIDR inside loopback, for example `127.0.0.1/32`, is more specific than go-libp2p's unlimited `127.0.0.0/8` entry, so it was matched first and capped loopback at the trusted limit. Loopback networks are now dropped from the trusted list, as loopback static peers already were.
- **Broadest-first order**: the two per-subnet lists are built in `ipBlockLimits`, and a test checks their prefix lengths (`[16 24 32]` and `[32 48 56]`). With narrowest first, a refusal leaves zero-count entries in go-libp2p's per-subnet maps until restart, and no test pinned the order before.
- **`ParseTrustedCIDRs` test**: `2001::/15` was rejected for its host bits, not for breadth. The test now uses `2000::/15`, so loosening the IPv6 bound makes it fail.
- **Refusal summary**: the interval is always one minute, so the parameter is gone and the message says "in the last minute"; `top` is now `mostRefusedBlocks` (also as the log key).
- **Wording**:
  - The ChangeLog entry and `configuring-erigon.mdx` now say that the /48 cap replaces go-libp2p's 64 and stays at most 64, that loopback stays unlimited when listed as trusted, and that trusted networks stay exempt with `--caplin.ip-block-limits.disable`.
  - The usage of `--caplin.ip-block-limits.disable` no longer names `--caplin.local-discovery`, which the standalone `caplin` binary does not have (there it is `--local-discovery`); it says "when local discovery is enabled".
  - `llms-full.txt` and `docs/site/static/llms-full.txt` are regenerated (`generate-llms.py --check` passes).

## Tests

- `TestIPBlockLimitsAreBroadestFirst` (new): the order of both lists, and the IPv6 /48 cap at 128, 512 and 1024 peers.
- `TestResourceManagerDoesNotCapLoopback`: a configuration that trusts `127.0.0.1/32` and `::1/128` with a trusted limit of 32. It opens 40 connections per address, alternating directions as before, so no direction goes above go-libp2p's transient limit on small machines. It fails without the loopback filter.
- `TestParseTrustedCIDRs`: `2000::/15`.

Mutation checks, each of which makes a test fail: the /48 cap without the bound, either list narrowest first, the loopback filter removed, and the IPv6 bound of `ParseTrustedCIDRs` loosened to 1.

The refusal summary change is a rename and a constant parameter with no behaviour change, so it has no new test; `TestRefusalCounterSummarisesRefusedBlocks` covers it.

`go test -race` passes for `cl/p2p/...`, `cl/sentinel/...`, `cmd/utils/...` and `cmd/caplin/...`. `make lint` is clean twice, and `make erigon integration` builds.
author: lystopad

title: cl/beacon/handler: accept SSZ in POST /eth/v2/validator/aggregate_and_proofs
body:
## Summary

`POST /eth/v1/validator/aggregate_and_proofs` and `POST /eth/v2/validator/aggregate_and_proofs` share one handler, which decoded only JSON. The [v2 Beacon API](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/master/apis/validator/aggregate_and_proofs.v2.yaml) also accepts an SSZ body (`application/octet-stream`), with the fork given by `Eth-Consensus-Version`.

The Prysm validator client sends this request as SSZ since OffchainLabs/prysm#17355, which is in Prysm v7.2.0 and v7.2.1. It switches to JSON only after an HTTP 415. Caplin answered 400 (`invalid character '\x04' looking for beginning of value`), so a Prysm validator client connected to Caplin never published an aggregate. This also affects mainnet nodes that pair Caplin, including `release/3.7`, with a Prysm v7.2.0 or later validator client.

Found in a local Kurtosis rehearsal of the Hoodi Glamsterdam fork: a Prysm validator client (`v7.3.0-rc.0`, `7e71942a`) on Caplin failed all 98 aggregate submissions. Its attestations, sync committee messages and payload attestations were not affected.

## Changes

- An `application/octet-stream` body is decoded as `List[SignedAggregateAndProof, MAX_COMMITTEES_PER_SLOT * TARGET_AGGREGATORS_PER_COMMITTEE]` for the fork in `Eth-Consensus-Version`, with a strict offset table for the outer list. A missing or unknown header returns 400. The body is limited to 32 MiB; the largest request the spec allows is about 17 MB.
- Every other content type is decoded as JSON, as before. A `Content-Type` header that does not parse now returns 415.
- Both routes get this behavior, because they share the handler.

## Tests

- `TestPoolAggregatesAndProofsAcceptsSSZ`: an SSZ request with `Eth-Consensus-Version: fulu` is processed, and the aggregate is published to gossip with its own SSZ encoding. On the old code it returns 400 with the error above.
author: domiwei

title: cl/beacon: declare application/json on JSON error responses
body:
## Summary

`EndpointError.WriteTo` wrote a JSON error body without a `Content-Type` header, and so did the pool failure responses. When no other code had set the header, `net/http` inferred `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`. The Nimbus validator client rejects such a response before it decodes the JSON body: it logs `Unable to decode error response: [Content-Type not supported]`, loses the error message, and reports the beacon node as having an unexpected status code or an incompatible configuration.

Found in a local Kurtosis rehearsal of the Hoodi Glamsterdam fork with a Nimbus validator client (`v26.10.0-e53a78`, unstable) on Caplin.

## Changes

- `EndpointError.WriteTo` and `writePoolingFailures` set `Content-Type: application/json` before the status code.
- The v1 and v2 attestation handlers and the payload attestation handler wrote the same failure response themselves. They now call `writePoolingFailures`.

## Tests

- New: `TestEndpointErrorWriteToDeclaresJSON` and `TestWritePoolingFailuresDeclaresJSON`.
- `TestPoolAttestationsDoNotPublishIgnored` (v1 and v2) and `TestPostPayloadAttestationsRejectsNullMessage` now also check the header.
- On the old code, `httptest.ResponseRecorder` records no `Content-Type`, so these checks fail; a real server would infer `text/plain`.
author: domiwei

title: cl/beacon/handler: serve next-epoch PTC duties while the head is in the previous epoch
body:
## Summary

Validator clients request PTC duties for epoch `N+1` at the start of epoch `N`, as the validator spec asks (`get_ptc_assignment` at the beginning of an epoch). At that moment the head is often still the last block of epoch `N-1`. Its `ptc_window` covers epochs `N-2` to `N` only. Caplin bounded the request by the head-state epoch and returned 400 (`PTC duties only available for current epoch N-1 and next epoch N, requested N+1`).

Found in a local Kurtosis rehearsal of the Hoodi Glamsterdam fork: after the fork, the Lighthouse validator client on Caplin got this 400 at every recorded epoch boundary, and the Nimbus validator client at most of them.

## Changes

- The upper bound now follows the Beacon API: the epoch must not be greater than the next epoch of the clock.
- When the requested epoch is two epochs ahead of the head state, a copy of the head state is advanced to the start of the epoch after the head state's epoch, and the duties come from its `ptc_window`. When the head is one epoch behind the clock, this is the clock's epoch. The copy is made inside the head-state view, and the epoch transition runs after the view is released.
  - `process_ptc_window` computes the PTC of `N+1` in the `N-1` to `N` transition, after `process_effective_balance_updates`. The dependent root of `N+1` is the block root at the last slot of `N-1`, so it covers every input. If a late block for that slot becomes canonical, the dependent root changes, and a validator client that follows the `head_v2` guidance of the [PTC duties API](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/master/apis/validator/duties/ptc.yaml) fetches the duties again.
  - Without the transition, `GetPTC` would fall back to `ComputePTC` on the head state, which uses the effective balances before the update.
- A request more than two epochs ahead of the head state, but not later than the clock's next epoch, returns 503.
- The fork-epoch rule from #24393 does not change: with the head in `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH - 1`, a request for `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH` still returns 503 without a transition. Once the clock reaches `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH` while the head is still in `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH - 1`, a request for `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH + 1` takes the new path, and the transition crosses the Gloas upgrade; its dependent root is the last slot of `GLOAS_FORK_EPOCH - 1`. No unit test covers this upgrade case.

## Tests

- `TestPostPtcDutiesNextEpochWhileHeadIsInPreviousEpoch`: the head is at the last slot of epoch `E` and the clock is in `E+1`; the request is for `E+2`. The expected duties come from a copy advanced with `ProcessSlots`. Half of the validators have a zero balance, so the effective balance update removes them from the PTC. The dependent root is the head root. On the old code the request returns 400; without the transition the duties differ.
- `TestPostPtcDutiesUnavailableWhileHeadLagsMoreThanOneEpoch`: a request three epochs ahead of the head state (the clock's next epoch while the head is two epochs behind) returns 503, and 500 without the guard.
author: domiwei

title: cl/phase1/forkchoice: export GLOAS weights in v1 debug fork choice
body:
`/eth/v1/debug/fork_choice` returns no current GLOAS nodes because `ForkNodes()` still reads the pre-GLOAS `f.weights` map, which `getHeadGloas` does not fill.

## Design

Under GLOAS, `ForkNodes()` exports the maintained GLOAS weight tree:

- **Refresh first.** `ForkNodes()` calls `GetHeadNode()` before it takes `f.mu.RLock`. When the head cache is valid this is the cheap read-lock fast path. When an input changed (vote, block, tick, payload decision, checkpoint update), it runs the same head computation the next `GetHead` would run, which prepares the tree. No lock is held during the call, so the lock order (`f.mu` before the synced-data lock) is kept.
- **Snapshot.** Each node in the prepared justified subtree, including the justified root, is exported with its aggregate PENDING attestation score. The proposer score is added to the boost root and its ancestors when `should_apply_proposer_boost` holds, which is what head selection uses for PENDING nodes. For siblings with 100 and 90 votes, a boost of 40 makes the second sibling's weight 130. Boost eligibility is checked once per snapshot, and only when the boost root's ancestry reaches an exported node. The snapshot never writes the head walk's boost cache.
- **Freshness guard.** The snapshot is empty when the tree has no checkpoint state, was prepared for a different justified checkpoint, or was pruned and not prepared again.
- **Prepare on the fallback head.** `computeHeadGloas` now prepares the tree before it returns the justified root as the fallback head when no leaf is viable. The returned head does not change. Without this, the export kept weights from an older preparation during a non-viability period.

Pre-GLOAS behavior is unchanged: `ForkNodes()` exports `f.weights` and does not refresh the head.

## Checkpoint-sync anchor

The fork graph has no per-root justified or finalized checkpoints for the checkpoint-sync anchor, so the anchor was dropped from the export. When the anchor is the store's justified root, `ForkNodes()` now uses the store's justified and finalized checkpoints for that node, as `get_forkchoice_store` initializes them from the anchor. The fork graph is not changed: `hasCorrectJustification` reads the same per-root checkpoints for viability filtering, so adding anchor metadata there would change head filtering. An anchor that is only an ancestor of the justified root is still skipped, as before.

## Known limits

All are limited to this debug endpoint:

- The refresh and the snapshot use two lock acquisitions. A checkpoint update or prune between them gives one empty response. A vote or block between them is missing from that response, and a parent can already carry the boost of a child that is not yet listed.
- When the justified checkpoint state cannot be loaded, the response is HTTP 200 with an empty `fork_choice_nodes`, not HTTP 500.
- After an epoch with no blocks, the anchor can report a justified epoch above its own.

The upstream API deprecates v1 for GLOAS. The v2 endpoint, where the checkpoints and nodes should come from one snapshot, is tracked in #24956.

This completes the v1 debug export deferred by #21913. Closes #21704.

## Testing

- `go test -race ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/` covers: the fork boundary (last pre-GLOAS slot exports `f.weights`, first GLOAS slot exports the tree), refresh of an unprepared or pruned tree, the pruned tree with a cached head, proposer boost inside and outside the subtree, the anchor as justified root and as an ancestor, and the fallback head with no viable leaf.
- `make lint` and `make erigon integration` pass.
- Two independent review rounds converged with no open in-scope findings.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/beacon: use Gloas preferences for proposer fee recipients
body:
Gloas block production ignores the fee recipient in signed proposer preferences. A proposer without a `prepare_beacon_proposer` registration therefore builds with the zero address, while a conflicting registration overrides the signed preference.

Use the preference matching the proposal slot, dependent root, and validator before falling back to `prepare_beacon_proposer`. An explicit zero address in a matching preference is valid. This precedence matches existing Gloas bid validation.

Production, configured builder bids, and background preparation share a non-logging fee resolver. Only production warns when neither source exists. Preparation reuses its registration lookup and records the effective recipient in its cache key so recipient changes trigger a new build. Preparation still requires a local validator registration.

Resolve the dependent root to the genesis block for epochs up to `MinSeedLookahead`, including when the head state is still at slot 0. This allows valid early-epoch preferences to supply the fee recipient and target gas limit on chains with Gloas active from genesis.

Regression tests failed before the fixes for production fee selection, preparation attributes, retrying after a recipient change, and genesis-epoch preference lookup. Coverage includes registration conflicts, explicit zero, unrelated preferences, the first Gloas slot, epochs 0 and 1, and the first proposal from a slot-0 state. Additional tests exercise repeated real preparation and compare the genesis root with actual slot processing. The resolver extraction, unused registration flag removal, and warning text update add no new behavior and use existing tests rather than new Red steps.

Fixes #23300.
author: yperbasis

title: cl: enable Gloas FULL-parent payload preparation
body:
Gloas envelope validation does not itself advance the execution layer's fork-choice head, so a direct FULL-parent build can remain unable to start before the proposal slot.

This PR lets the canonical ForkChoice stage react to execution-head changes even when the beacon root stays the same. Payload preparation can then warm a verified FULL-parent builder. Priming is best-effort; normal production sends its own FCU and remains the fallback.

Fixes #23551.
Fixes #25141.

## Design

- **Before Gloas:** the canonical stage continues to send `FCU(GetEth1Hash(headRoot))` on every pass.
- **Gloas execution head:** root, slot and payload status come from the complete snapshot returned by `GetHeadWithSyncedHeadState`, with `GetHeadNode` as the fallback when the head state is not synced. FULL maps to `bid.BlockHash`; EMPTY and PENDING map to `bid.ParentBlockHash`. The snapshot may use or refresh the head cache; the hash mapping reads the block's bid rather than the `eth2Roots` LRU. Unresolved or pre-Gloas blocks fall back to `GetEth1Hash`.
- **Canonical FCU does not require prior payload verification.** An accepted but unverified FULL head still receives an FCU, allowing the EL to advance and verify later payloads.
- **Wake detection:** `cfg.executionHead` records the canonical decision, including after tolerated FCU timeouts—not confirmed EL adoption. SleepForSlot wakes for a changed beacon root or execution-head decision, not cache invalidation alone. The wake throttle follows the stage's decision even when it differs from the triggering poll; fatal FCU errors leave both records unchanged. Same-root execution-head changes bypass the one-second wake limit in both directions, so FULL-to-EMPTY can move the EL back to `bid.ParentBlockHash`. Polls recheck cancellation and the next-slot deadline after each blocking head read.
- **Preparation requires a verified FULL parent.** It quietly skips unverified FULL payloads and rechecks the selected root, payload path and FULL verification before each builder attempt and before recording the payload ID. Preparation never sends an FCU. A proposer-specific FULL-to-EMPTY decision waits for production's FCU.

## Limits and follow-ups

- A busy direct EL can drop an FCU without payload attributes while the client reports success. The stage records that decision, so an unchanged decision does not trigger an in-slot resend. Production still sends its own FCU. Existing non-fatal handling of MissingSegment, TooFarAway and ReorgTooDeep is unchanged.
- Late verification or a transient skip after the PTC deadline can leave too little time before the next preparation tick.
- While ChainTipSync waits after a missed slot, a same-root payload-status change may go unnoticed until the next block.
- Post-publication adoption still sends `GetEth1Hash(headRoot)`. SleepForSlot compares canonical decisions, not the actual EL head, so it does not guarantee correction of an EL-only head change. The publication hash and inherited execution-hash placeholder are tracked in #25285.
- Loaded Gloas FULL-parent performance has not been measured. The integration tests prove warmup and reuse, not a net CPU, memory or proposal-latency improvement. The A/B measurement is tracked in #24119, item 3.

## Verification

- Tests verify that the synced-head lookup preserves FULL, EMPTY and PENDING payload status.
- Tests cover execution-hash resolution, repeated pre-Gloas FCUs, Gloas FULL/EMPTY decisions, unresolved-head fallback, timeout/fatal-error handling, and same-root FULL/EMPTY changes in both directions.
- Virtual-time tests cover a stage decision that differs from the triggering poll, plus cancellation or slot expiry during either head read.
- Real-store and execution-module tests cover unverified FULL-head advancement, payload invalidation and head changes. The warmup test exercises SSZ gossip decoding, service validation, the canonical ForkChoice stage, preparation, production and collection. It checks canonical/materialized/EL heads, pre-slot warmup and payload-ID reuse.
- Collection tests cover prepared, absent, mismatched and failed primes. Tests that wait for real slot timing use the `testing.Short()` long-running-test guard.
- `make lint`, `make erigon integration`, and race-detector tests in the handler, fork-choice, stages and execution-client packages pass.
author: yperbasis

title: cl, execution: complete payload preparation coverage and hardening
body:
Closes #23419.

Complete the remaining payload preparation hardening, and prove that normal block production collects the prepared execution build only when its payload ID matches. Missing, failed, skipped and mismatched preparation keep the normal collection window.

## Changes

**Real-module coverage**
- 22 handler-to-execution-module cases: ordinary pre-Gloas slots, pre-Fulu epoch boundaries, the first Gloas slot and EMPTY cover prepared, absent, failed and mismatched preparation. FULL and FULL-to-EMPTY cover intentional preparation skips, absent records and mismatched records.
- Each case checks the collected ID, the execution parent, collection timing, and that preparation leaves the source state's slot unchanged.
- The matrix uses a shared fixture and a case table. It runs in the full suite behind the canonical `testing.Short()` guard.
- Naming changes, the metric refactor and documentation edits skip TDD because they do not change behavior; existing tests and documentation checks cover them.

**Import coordination**
- Builder startup is coordinated with canonical imports by slot. An import that starts cancels a running speculative startup. Preparation is refused while an import in its slot range is registered.
- Import registrations:
  - block imports (`onBlock`, `processAndStoreBlock`);
  - envelope imports, registered after the builder signature check and keyed by the known block slot;
  - envelope consensus validation;
  - the stage `NewPayloadWithAdmission` path.
- Queued gossip blocks hold no import claim before the expected proposer is checked:
  - A gossip block parked before its proposer is verified holds no claim. Unknown parents leave the job queued without taking validation capacity or accessing state. Parents at the same or a later slot cause terminal rejection before state access. The retry checks the expected proposer before starting an import. Missing parent state leaves the job queued without cancelling preparation; a wrong proposer removes the job. A block with the expected proposer retains its claim if processing returns a dependency or back-off error.
  - Blocks parked after full gossip validation (data availability, parent envelope pending, too early, back-off) and locally published blocks keep their claim between retries until the job is removed or expires.
- Envelopes queued in the gossip service because their block is unknown register their root until the job is removed or expires. They refuse preparation only once that root is a known block in range, and the registration never cancels a running attempt. Envelopes queued on admission-busy are not registered: the in-flight envelope for the same block and builder claims after authentication, and so does the queued one when it is processed.
- Envelopes parked in fork choice count only for blocks after the selected head. The selected head's own parked envelope may never import (for example, withheld data columns), so preparation still primes its EMPTY fallback, as before. Persisted envelopes (index-repair markers) never count.

**Builder ID, metrics and flag**
- Deadline expiry alone does not discard a successful builder startup result. Import interruption is tracked independently of context cancellation and prevents recording the attempt as prepared even if the deadline fired first. A changed selected head also prevents recording it as prepared.
- `caplin_payload_preparation_outcomes_total{outcome}` uses a fixed set of reasons. New labels:
  - `too_early`;
  - `busy` when the wait is caused by block processing;
  - the cancellation cause from admission (`busy` for an import, `late` for the deadline).
- The PTC wait counts `pending` once.
- `caplin_payload_preparation_collections_total{outcome="reused|absent|mismatch"}` reports whether collection reused a matching prepared payload. `absent` also covers disabled or unsupported preparation.
- `--caplin.payload-preparation.disable` covers embedded and standalone Caplin and disables preparation without disabling the validator API or normal block production. Preparation is enabled by default when the validator API is enabled and the execution client supports direct payload building. The flag path logs once.

**Builder reuse, cache and payload IDs**
- An exact live execution builder is reused after an A → B → A head flip, with the existing bounded eviction.
- Decoded FULL-parent execution requests are cached for up to eight roots. The LRU is built in the constructor, and concurrent misses are coalesced, so a root is decoded at most once while it is retained.
- Deterministic slot-transition and withdrawal derivation failures are memoized for the whole preparation key. Cancellation, contention, storage and EL failures stay retryable.
- Engine API payload-ID decoding is shared with the hybrid client: big-endian, and exactly eight bytes. The direct client's wire format is unchanged.

## Known limitations

- FULL and FULL-to-EMPTY are intentional preparation skips with successful normal FCU and collection coverage. FULL priming is tracked in #23551. #24938 lands after this PR and flips those matrix cases.
- After the PTC deadline, an attempt refused because an import is in progress waits for the next quarter-slot tick. This is the bounded post-PTC retry of #24119 item 2.
- The import claim ends when fork choice has processed the block, before the stage publishes the new head. A late block can therefore let preparation build briefly on the old head. This heals on the next tick.
- `onBlock` registers its import on entry, before validation, so a block that turns out invalid can cancel a running attempt for the length of that call.
- A gossip-verified block parked on data availability or a missing parent envelope (`ErrParentEnvelopePending`) can hold its claim until the 30 s job expiry. Withheld columns, or a parent envelope available to the next proposer but not to us, can suppress our preparation for the next slot or two.
- While a claim covers the range, each tick repeats the state copy before admission is refused.
- An unauthenticated envelope queued for a block that is not yet known refuses preparation for one queue pass after that block becomes known.
- After an A → B → A builder reuse, the collections metric can report `mismatch` although production reused a warm builder.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/phase1/forkchoice: remove per-step trace logs from parent payload status
body:
## Summary

On Gloas, fork-choice ancestor walks allocated memory on every step between two Gloas blocks, even with trace logging disabled. The same walk on Fulu allocates nothing.

`ParentPayloadStatusFromBids` (`cl/phase1/forkchoice/payload_vote.go`) ended with a `log.Trace` call on both the FULL and the EMPTY result. `common/log/v3` builds the record before the level filter drops it (`logger.write` creates the `*Record` and copies the context; `lvlFilterHandler` checks the level afterwards). So every call that reached the bid hash comparison allocated the record, a context slice, a boxed slot and two (FULL) or three (EMPTY) boxed `common.Hash` values: 5 allocations / 296 B on FULL and 6 allocations / 360 B on EMPTY for slots of 256 and above (smaller slots are boxed without allocating).

`getAncestor` calls the function through `getParentPayloadStatus` on every step between two Gloas blocks. Gossip validation of an attestation or an aggregate walks up to twice (target checkpoint and finalized checkpoint), fork choice walks as well, and the Gloas weight tree and the `execution_payload_envelopes_by_range` handler also call the function.

Measured cost of a 64-step `Ancestor` walk (local benchmark, Apple M5 Pro, go1.26.8, benchstat, n=10):

| walk | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Gloas | 7.55 µs, 20.5 KiB, 352 allocs | 1.55 µs, 0 B, 0 allocs |
| Fulu | 1.39 µs, 0 B, 0 allocs | 1.40 µs, 0 B, 0 allocs |

That is about 118 ns and 5.5 allocations (328 B) per step before, and about 24 ns and no allocations after, close to Fulu's 22 ns.

Estimated impact on mainnet once Gloas is active (about 1M validators): a gossip attestation or aggregate that passes both ancestry checks walks about 95 steps in total (vote for a block in the current slot, a block in every slot, finality two epochs back), so the trace calls cost about 520 allocations, 31 KB and 9 µs per message. With about 85 aggregates per second (64 committees per slot, 16 target aggregators each) and up to 250 attestations per 6-second window, about 42 per second on average (attestation gossip is capped for all subnets together by `withGlobalTimeBasedRateLimiter` in `cl/phase1/network/registry/register.go`), that is about 4 MB/s of short-lived garbage and about 66k allocations per second, before fork-choice walks.

The fix removes both trace calls instead of guarding them with a level check. They printed the slot, the two bid hashes (equal on FULL) and, on EMPTY, the parent root, all of which are in the blocks themselves, and with trace on they would print a line on every walk step.

## Not changed here

- `common/log/v3` still builds every record before the level filter; other `log.Trace`/`log.Debug` calls on other paths still allocate when filtered out.
- The walk benchmark is a local harness and is not added to the repository; the new test guards the allocation-free behaviour.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/payload_vote.go`: remove the two `log.Trace` calls in `ParentPayloadStatusFromBids` and the now unused `log` import. The comparison and the returned statuses are unchanged.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/payload_vote_test.go`: add `TestParentPayloadStatusFromBidsDoesNotAllocate`.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestParentPayloadStatusFromBidsDoesNotAllocate` builds a Gloas parent and child and checks, for a FULL and an EMPTY pair, the returned status and `testing.AllocsPerRun(1000, ...) == 0`. With the production file from `main` it fails with 5 allocations (full) and 6 (empty); with this change it passes, also with `-race` and `-cover`.
- Benchmark: the table above; a 65-block chain (64 steps, half FULL and half EMPTY) in an in-memory fork graph, `ForkChoiceStore.Ancestor` from the head to the first block, `-benchmem`, before and after runs interleaved.
- `go test -p 2 -count=1 ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/...`, `go test -race -p 2 -count=1 ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/`, `make lint`, `make erigon integration`.
author: domiwei

title: cl/beacon/handler: collect unprepared Gloas payloads at a third of the attestation window
body:
## Summary

After the Gloas fork, Lighthouse finished verifying Caplin's gossip blocks about 2.2 s into the slot. In Gloas a block counts as timely only if it is from the current slot and arrives before the attestation deadline (`ATTESTATION_DUE_BPS_GLOAS`, 3 s with 12-second slots). A late block cannot get the proposer boost, and if it is also weak, the next proposer may re-org it (`get_proposer_head`, which checks several more conditions). At 2.2 s, little time is left for the block to reach the rest of the network.

In a local Kurtosis rehearsal of the Hoodi Glamsterdam fork (no added network latency), Lighthouse verified the gossip blocks after the fork at these times into the slot:

| proposer | blocks | median | p90 (nearest rank) | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| erigon + Caplin | 93 | 2234 ms | 2250 ms | 2431 ms |
| geth + Prysm | 46 | 55 ms | 70 ms | 124 ms |
| nethermind + Teku | 54 | 30 ms | 34 ms | 48 ms |
| geth + Nimbus | 65 | 80 ms | 93 ms | 586 ms |

## Why

- Gloas payload preparation stands down when the parent is FULL or FULL-to-EMPTY (`gloasPathRequiresForkChoiceUpdate`, #23436): both need production's normal FCU, because preparation uses `StartPayloadBuild`, which cannot change fork choice. In the rehearsal FULL was the usual case.
- So the builder starts with the production FCU, and an unprepared payload is collected in a window that ends at `attestationDue - attestationDue/4` (#21989): first poll at 2.15 s, deadline 2.25 s in Gloas.
- In the rehearsal, 67 of 70 `BlockProduction: ForkChoiceUpdate&GetPayload took` records after the fork were above 2 s.

## Changes

- An unprepared Gloas payload is now collected in a window that ends at a third of the attestation window: first poll at 0.9 s, deadline 1 s with 12-second slots (the retry window stays 100 ms). These are nominal times; the FCU or a running `GetAssembledBlock` call can take longer.
- An unprepared Gloas production that starts late gets a later deadline: 500 ms after the time taken just before its FCU, capped at the prepared deadline (2.25 s in Gloas). The FCU itself uses part of this time. As before, the first poll is never earlier than the request, so a request that comes in after the deadline is polled once, right away. Without the later deadline, a late start (a slow FCU, state work at an epoch boundary, a late request from the validator client) would stop the builder at once and publish an almost empty payload.
- A prepared payload (an exact payload-ID match with warmup) can still be retried until 2.25 s. Its first poll is the earlier of the prepared first poll (0.65 s after at least 1.5 s of warmup) and the unprepared one, so a payload prepared late is first polled no later than an unprepared one.
- The wait for a parked parent envelope from #24832 now uses the prepared collection point, so its cutoff stays at 1.5 s with 12-second slots instead of moving to 0.25 s.
- Blocks before Gloas are unchanged.

Trade-off: on a FULL parent the builder now has about 1 s instead of about 2.2 s to fill the payload. Preparing the payload on a FULL parent would remove this trade-off, but it needs a change to the preparation design and is not part of this PR.

## Tests

These window tests now expect the new unprepared Gloas values, and fail on the old code:
- `TestBlockBuilderWindowGloas`
- `TestBlockBuilderWindowReservesPublicationMargin`
- `TestBlockBuilderWindowTakesPreparedPayloadEarly`: it also checks that the prepared Gloas window stays at 0.65 s to 2.25 s.

`TestMaximumPreparedAdvancePreservesRecentBuildTime` now also checks that the Gloas advance cap stays 1.5 s.

New tests, which fail on the earlier version of this PR:
- `TestBlockBuilderWindowGloasLateStartKeepsMinimumBuildTime`: a production that starts at 1.3 s is first polled at 1.7 s with a deadline of 1.8 s; one that starts at 2 s is capped at 2.15 s and 2.25 s.
- `TestBlockBuilderWindowShortGloasWarmupPollsNoLaterThanUnprepared`: with 500 ms of warmup the first poll is at 0.9 s, and the polling cutoff stays at 2.25 s.

These tests cover the window arithmetic only, not how full a payload is after 1 s of building.
author: domiwei

title: cl/phase1/network/services: process attestations and aggregates whose block arrives later
body:
## Summary

An attestation or aggregate that names a block fork choice has not imported yet was ignored and dropped. The p2p spec allows a client to queue such messages until the block is retrieved. When a block arrives a few seconds late, votes for it received in between are lost, which can leave fork choice on a different head than the rest of the network.

Found in a local Kurtosis rehearsal of the Hoodi Glamsterdam fork (erigon with embedded Caplin, next to Lighthouse, Teku, Prysm and Nimbus):
- The block of slot 443 reached Lighthouse and two other Caplin nodes at about 13:42:01.1 UTC. The affected node imported it only at 13:42:07.07; at 13:42:01.001 its log shows the envelope of the parent (slot 442) still waiting for data columns.
- Teku and the Lighthouse validator client published attestations for 443 at about 13:42:01.1, before the affected node had the block.
- At the start of slot 444 the node's fork-choice head was 442, while the other clients' head was 443. The node's own proposal for 444 then failed with `fork choice head changed: proposal parent <443>, current head <442>`, and slot 445 built on 443.
- IGNORE results are logged at trace level, so the captured debug logs do not show whether the node received or ignored those votes; that is inferred from the timing and the old code. The observed head of 442 is consistent with those votes not being applied.

The old attestation scheduler was disabled in #12830; it scanned every stored attestation on each tick, had no size limit, and did not store the subnet. In the aggregate service the "block not seen" check ran after the finalized-ancestor check, which an unknown block fails once the finalized checkpoint is not genesis, so the check was not reached.

## Changes

- A gossip message that reaches the unknown-block check still returns IGNORE and is not forwarded. If the queue has room, it is kept per block root, and if a queue check sees the block while the entry has not expired, the message runs again through `ProcessMessage`, with the normal validation and the existing proposer gate.
- The aggregate service checks that the block is known before the finalized-ancestor check.
- REST submissions (`ImmediateProcess`) are not queued.
- The attestation service and the aggregate service each have their own queue:
  - A 100 ms ticker checks it with one `GetHeader` call per unexpired queued root. A check that releases replays waits for them, so the next check can start later.
  - At most 32 distinct pending roots. This is an implementation cap, not a protocol bound; once it is full, further roots are not queued. Messages are queued before signature verification, so gossip with made-up roots can fill the queue; votes for additional roots are then dropped as before, until the made-up entries expire.
  - At most 32768 pending attestations or `MAX_COMMITTEES_PER_SLOT * TARGET_AGGREGATORS_PER_COMMITTEE` (1024 on mainnet) pending aggregates; replays already released are outside these caps. 32768 is about the single attestations of one slot with one million active validators (1,000,000 / 32).
  - A root becomes eligible for expiry once it has been queued for longer than one slot, and is removed on a later check; replay work can delay that check.
  - Up to `batchSignatureVerificationThreshold` replays run at the same time, because a replay that reaches signature verification waits for its batch. Concurrent replays go through the same seen-message checks as concurrent gossip validation.
- The disabled scheduler of the attestation service and the aggregate retry loop, which nothing fed, are removed.

Not changed here:
- The queue waits for the block only. A Gloas vote with `data.index == 1` whose payload is not verified yet is still ignored and not queued (the Gloas p2p spec also allows queuing it until the payload is retrieved).
- Gossip single attestations go to the local aggregation path and the event emitter, not to fork choice directly, and from Fulu on, gossip aggregates reach fork choice only when a local validator proposes in the current or next epoch (#18521); REST submissions bypass that check.

## Tests

- `TestAttestationForLateBlockIsProcessedOnceBlockArrives` and `TestAggregateAndProofForLateBlockIsProcessedOnceBlockArrives`: a message for an unknown root is processed after the block becomes known. Both fail on the old code.
- `TestBlockArrivalQueueDropsReplaysBeyondCapacity`, `TestBlockArrivalQueueDropsRootsBeyondCapacity`, `TestBlockArrivalQueueFreesCapacityAfterReplay` and `TestBlockArrivalQueueDropsExpiredReplays` cover the queue's capacity, root cap, capacity reuse and expiry.
author: domiwei

title: cl/das: follow-ups to the deferred column sync
body:
Follow-up to #24830 (Part of #24620). It addresses the non-blocking points from @domiwei's approval of #24830.

## Changes

- **Worker tick:** the tick was one second. It is now a quarter of the shortest custody grace, between 100 ms and 1 s: 375 ms on mainnet, and about 156 ms with five-second slots (Gnosis, Chiado). Before, on Gnosis a due root could be picked up up to 1 s late, while the grace is 833 ms and the attestation deadline is 1666 ms.
- **Gloas grace:** before Gloas, custody columns decide the attestation to the block, so the grace is half the time to the attestation deadline. From Gloas they decide the envelope and the PTC's `blob_data_available` vote, and a root is queued when its envelope is processed. So the grace is now half the window from `PAYLOAD_DUE_BPS` to the PTC deadline. With the current constants the value does not change: 1.5 s on mainnet.
- **First attempt computed once:** `SyncColumnDataLater` computes the first attempt as the later of the slot start and now, plus the delay, and stores it as `nextAttempt`. `due` only compares `nextAttempt` with now. `queuedAt`, `deferredColumnSyncDue` and the callbacks that computed the same deadline on every tick are removed. Behaviour is unchanged.
- **Comments:** `queued` moves into the test file. The comment at the backoff cap now says that nothing in the queue queues a root again, but a later `SyncColumnDataLater` can, for example the retry of a parked Gloas envelope.

Not in this PR: the Gloas EMPTY-payload cutoff and the per-peer pacing of by-root requests. They are items four and five of #24789.

## Tests

- `TestSyncColumnDataWorkerKeepsACanonicalRootAtTheBackoffCap`: the reverse of the orphan test. The root is canonical at its slot and reaches a second attempt.
- `TestDeferredColumnSyncTick`: mainnet and five-second-slot values.
- `TestSyncColumnDataWorkerPicksADueRootUpWithinTheTick`: with five-second slots, a due root is picked up within the tick.
- `TestSyncColumnDataLaterSchedulesTheFirstAttempt`: the first attempt counts from the later of the slot start and the enqueue, and queuing the root again keeps it. It replaces the `deferredColumnSyncDue` tests.
- The worker tests use `fuluColumnBlock`. The two sentinel fakes are one fake with an `active` count.

Mutation checks (each makes a test fail):
- dropping the canonical check at the cap;
- a fixed one-second tick;
- a different tick fraction;
- a first attempt that ignores the slot start;
- `due` ignoring `nextAttempt`;
- queuing again overwriting the first attempt.

Replacing the Gloas grace with half the Gloas attestation deadline passes: with the current constants both are 25% of the slot.

There is still no worker-level test of the custody round (`DownloadOnlyCustodyColumns`). It needs custody state and a peer that serves columns, which would make this PR much larger.

`go test -race` passes for `cl/das/...`, `cl/phase1/network/services/...` and `cl/phase1/forkchoice/...`, and the worker tests pass 10 times with `-race`. `make lint` reports 0 issues twice, and `make erigon integration` builds.
author: lystopad

title: cl/aggregation: count each committee member's vote once
body:
Follow-up to #24813, from @domiwei's review of it.

## Problem

In a committee with a local aggregator, the pool keeps aside up to `MAX_VALIDATORS_PER_COMMITTEE` refused data, so every data that got a vote keeps it. That relies on each member voting once per epoch, and nothing enforced it. `validatorAttestationSeen` keeps only the last target epoch per validator (#24824), so a validator that alternates votes for two target epochs gets every vote claimed, and each new vote can carry new data. One such validator could fill the refused set of a duty committee to 2048 data. Each new data then cost about 240 µs under the pool lock, and honest one-vote data could be evicted. The double votes are slashable, but the pool's guarantee did not hold.

## Change

- A member votes once per epoch, in one slot and committee. The pool now records the members whose vote it counts, per slot and committee (`voters`). A vote of a member already counted for other data of the committee is refused with `ErrVoterAlreadyCounted`, both for stored data and for data kept aside. A vote for data that already holds the member is still `ErrIsSuperset`.
- So every data needs its own voter: the data of a committee never outnumber its members, and the bound for duty committees holds by construction. The comment on `refusedLimit` now says `MAX_VALIDATORS_PER_COMMITTEE` instead of "the committee size".
- The counted members are pruned with the inclusion window.
- The attestation service logs `ErrVoterAlreadyCounted` at Debug, like `ErrPoolLimit`, and still emits the attestation event.

This also covers the duty case of #24824 at the pool. The seen-cache key in #24824 itself does not change here.

## Tests

- `TestAddAttestationElectraRefusesAMemberAlreadyCountedForOtherData`: a second vote of a member for other data is refused, for stored and refused data; the same vote again is still `ErrIsSuperset`.
- `TestAddAttestationElectraEquivocatingMemberCannotFlushALocalAggregatorsData`: in a full duty committee, one member voting for 100 new data adds none of them, and the honest data kept aside stays.
- `TestPruneStaleDropsCountedMembers`.
- `TestAddAggregatorDutyKeepsOnlyDutiesInTheWindow` now also keeps a duty of the previous epoch through the prune.
- `TestAttestationOfACountedMemberIsNotAWarning` (services): the event is emitted and nothing is logged at Warn.
- Three existing pool tests used one member's vote for several data of a committee, which an honest committee does not produce. They now give each data its own voters; their assertions do not change.

The new pool tests failed before the change. Mutation checks: removing the member check, not recording members, dropping the exemption for the member's own data, not looking up the refused data, not pruning the members, pruning previous-epoch duties, and logging the new error at Warn each fail a test.

`BenchmarkAddAttestationElectra` (425 single votes, real BLS, `-count 5`): about 10.60 ms/op on `main` and 10.64 ms/op here, 9371 and 10223 allocs/op.

`go test -race` passes for `cl/aggregation/...`, `cl/phase1/network/services/...`, `cl/beacon/handler/...` and `cl/validator/...`; `make lint` is clean twice.
author: lystopad

title: cl/beacon/handler: verify the selected attestations against the proposal state
body:
Fixes #24826.

## Problem

Block production does not verify the attestations it packs: `processBlockForProduction` runs the transition without `FullValidation`. Aggregation bit positions are mapped to validators with the head-state committees when an attestation is received. After a reorg that changes the shuffling, a packed attestation can be invalid for the proposal state, and then our own block is invalid. Gossip aggregates already go through this path, and since #24813 local aggregates do too.

## Change

After `selectAttestations` picks at most `MAX_ATTESTATIONS` (8 from Electra, 128 before), `findBestAttestationsForBlockProduction` verifies each selected attestation against the proposal state, as block processing would: attesting indices from the proposal state, then `IsValidIndexedAttestation`, which checks the indices and the aggregate signature. An attestation that fails is dropped with a warning; the rest of the block is unchanged.

From Electra, aggregates of the same data from several committees are merged into one attestation. If one committee fails, the merged attestation is dropped with it. The block stays valid; this is a backstop for a rare case, so it does not re-split or re-select.

## Cost

`BenchmarkVerifySelectedAttestations` (new, `_bench_test.go`): a full Electra block, 8 attestations of 64 committees of 512 signers each, with the decompressed public keys cached as Caplin runs them (`bls.SetEnabledCaching(true)`). About 143 ms per block on a 16-core dev machine. This runs in the operations goroutine of `produceBeaconBody`, in parallel with the payload goroutine, which collects the payload about 0.65 to 0.9 s into the slot. Today the operations goroutine takes a few ms, so the check stays off the critical path. Verifying the 8 attestations in parallel saved only about 30 ms, so it is sequential. Before Electra a block holds up to 128 single-committee attestations; each check is cheaper there (one committee of signers), and all current networks are past Electra.

## Tests

- `TestFindBestAttestationsDropsAttestationsThatFailAgainstTheProposalState`: real BLS keys and signing roots behind a mocked proposal state that rotates one committee's members, as a changed shuffling would. The attestation of that committee is dropped, the other one is packed.
- `TestFindBestAttestationsDropsAMergedAttestationWithAFailingCommittee`: the merged attestation is dropped as a whole.
- `TestFindBestAttestationsKeepsAttestationsThatVerify`: valid attestations are packed as before.

The first two failed before the change. Packing the selection unchecked, or checking the indices without the signature, fails them again.

`go test -race` passes for `cl/beacon/handler/...` and `cl/phase1/core/state/...`; `make lint` is clean twice.
author: lystopad

title: cl/phase1/execution_client: back off the direct payload build retry from 10 ms
body:
Fixes #24964.

## Change

`retryAssembleBlock` now waits 10 ms before the first retry and doubles the delay up to the previous 200 ms cap, with the same 30 attempts. The direct forkchoice update answers before its commit releases the execution semaphore, so the `AssembleBlock` that follows it is usually busy for tens of milliseconds. A fixed 200 ms wait made almost every production start its payload build about 200 ms late; on a Gloas FULL parent, where preparation does not run, that time came out of the building window.

## Measurements

A Sepolia node (Gloas, embedded Caplin) at the chain head, asked for an unsigned block at the start of the slot:

| | productions | wait before the build starts (p50 / p90 / max) |
|---|---|---|
| fixed 200 ms (`main`) | 328 | 200 / 200 / 1003 ms |
| this change | 32 | 71 / 151 / 312 ms |

The payload is collected at the same time either way (about 2.1 s into the slot), so the saving is building time.

## Tests

- `TestAssembleRetryDelayBacksOffToTheCap`: 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, then 200 ms.
- `TestRetryAssembleBlockRetriesOneBusyAnswerQuickly`: one busy answer costs the first delay, not the cap. With a fixed delay at the cap it fails.
- The existing retry tests pass with both delays.

`go test -race ./cl/phase1/execution_client/...` passes; `make lint` is clean twice.
author: lystopad

title: cl/das, cl/phase1/stages: backfill custody columns of forward-synced blocks
body:
Part of #24704.

## Problem

Forward sync imports blocks with `checkDataAvailability = false`, so it never fetches or queues their data columns. The deferred column sync (`syncColumnDataWorker`) only learns about roots from the data checks on the gossip and chain-tip import paths. A node that forward-synced through Fulu or Gloas slots, for example after downtime, therefore kept a custody gap for those blocks for the whole data-column serve range. It answered `DataColumnSidecarsByRange`/`ByRoot` for them with a partial set, which peers score down.

## Change

- When forward sync finishes, or hands off to chain-tip sync after stalling, it calls `PeerDas.BackfillCustodyColumns(startSlot, highestProcessed)`. The call returns at once; a request that comes while another one waits is merged into it.
- A PeerDAS worker runs the backfill:
  - It waits until the canonical chain in the beacon indices reaches the end of the range. Forward sync stores its blocks before the fork choice stage marks them canonical. After two epochs it stops waiting and walks what is marked.
  - It walks the canonical roots from the newest slot down, clipped to the data-column serve range, so the most recent blocks are served first.
  - It reads each block without its execution payload (`ReadBeaconBlockBodyBySlot`), and takes the root from the canonical index.
  - It queues a block that commits to blobs and whose columns are not available for the existing column sync worker, due at once. That worker already handles download rounds, retries with backoff, giving up orphans, and the serve-range cutoff.
- Queue entries are light (`backfillColumnBlock`: version, slot, root, commitments, signature), not whole blocks.
- The backfill waits while the column sync queue holds 32 roots below the maximum backoff. It neither crowds out the roots gossip queues nor asks peers for a whole range at once, and roots at the maximum backoff, which may never complete, do not stall it.
- A root the backfill queued is given up when its backoff reaches an epoch, so roots peers cannot serve do not pile up. The stale forward-sync handoff covers blocks up to the highest seen slot.
- A Gloas block is queued only once its envelope was processed: without a revealed payload no columns exist. Nothing is walked before Fulu, and the walk stops when its context ends.

Not covered: a restart during a backfill does not resume it. The next forward sync only covers its own range. Resuming would need a persisted cursor.

Related: #24787 (`earliest_available_slot` and the stored custody columns), #24789 (per-peer pacing of by-root requests).

## Tests

- `TestBackfillCustodyColumnsQueuesBlocksMissingColumns`: only blocks in the range with blob commitments and missing columns are queued, with the canonical root and due at once.
- `TestBackfillCustodyColumnsQueuesNewestFirstWithinItsBound`: at most 32 roots, newest first.
- Added after review: `...SkipsGloasBlocksWithoutAnEnvelope`, `...IsNotStalledByRootsAtTheMaximumBackoff`, `...MergesWaitingRequests` (replaces the drop test), `...StopsWhenCancelled`, `...DoesNothingBeforeFulu`.
- `TestBackfillCustodyColumnsSkipsSlotsBelowTheServeRange`.
- `TestBackfillCustodyColumnsWaitsForTheCanonicalChain`: the walk starts only once the canonical chain reaches the range end.
- `TestBackfillCustodyColumnsRequestIsAsynchronous`.
- `TestRequestCustodyBackfillAsksForTheImportedRange` (stages): the range is requested, and an empty one is not.

Each fails with its rule removed: the serve-range clamp, the bound, the newest-first walk, the canonical wait, queueing available blocks too, and the empty-range check in the stage helper.

`go test -race` passes for `cl/das/...`, `cl/phase1/stages/...`, `cl/phase1/network/...` and `cl/phase1/forkchoice/...`; `make lint` is clean twice; `make erigon integration` builds.
author: lystopad

title: cl/phase1/network/registry: scale the attestation gossip budget with expected traffic
body:
## Summary

Caplin admits attestation gossip through one node-wide budget of 250 messages per 6-second fixed window (`withGlobalTimeBasedRateLimiter(6*time.Second, 250)` in `cl/phase1/network/registry/register.go`). The budget is shared by all peers, all 64 `beacon_attestation_{subnet_id}` topics and, during a fork transition, both fork digests. It is checked before the message is decoded, and a message over the budget gets `ValidationIgnore`: Caplin does not process it and gossipsub does not forward it. go-libp2p-pubsub marks a message as seen before it runs the validator, so copies of an ignored attestation from other peers are dropped as duplicates.

From Electra on, every attester publishes one `SingleAttestation`, so a subnet carries active validators / (32 x 64) attestations per slot: about 408 on mainnet (835,924 active validators) and about 559 on Hoodi (1,144,656). Attesters broadcast when the slot's block arrives or at the attestation deadline, whichever comes first. If all of a slot's attestations land in one 6-second window, the node drops:

| Subscribed subnets | Mainnet | Hoodi |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 39% | 55% |
| 2 | 69% | 78% |
| 64 (`--caplin.subscribe-all-topics`) | 99% | 99% |

A validator node subscribes to the subnets of its validators' duties. The dropped attestations are not relayed to the node's mesh peers, they do not reach the aggregation pool, so the aggregates built for local aggregators miss them, and event stream subscribers do not see them.

The budget comes from #12830 and was moved before decoding in #17606. Its purpose is to bound the CPU and memory Caplin spends on attestation gossip. This PR keeps it for that purpose but sizes it from the traffic the node should receive. At the start of each window the budget is set to max(250, 3/2 x expected), both values rounded down, where

expected = S x N x B / (SLOTS_PER_EPOCH x ATTESTATION_SUBNET_COUNT)

- S is the number of attestation subnets the node is subscribed to. It counts distinct subnet ids of topics that are actually subscribed, so a subnet subscribed under both fork digests during a fork transition counts once (the traffic moves from one digest to the other, it does not double), and joined but unsubscribed topics do not count (gossipsub does not deliver their messages).
- N is the number of active validators in the head state, 0 without a head state, so the budget is then 250.
- B is the number of slots whose burst can fall into the 6-second window, ceil(6 s / SECONDS_PER_SLOT): 1 for 12-second slots, 2 on Gnosis and Chiado (5-second slots).

Resulting budgets per window:

| Network | Active validators | S = 1 | S = 2 | S = 64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Mainnet | 835,924 | 612 | 1,224 | 39,183 |
| Hoodi | 1,144,656 | 837 | 1,675 | 53,655 |
| Sepolia | ~1,782 | 250 | 250 | 250 |
| Small devnet (mainnet or minimal preset) | 64 to 512 | 250 | 250 | 250 |

Sepolia and small devnets keep 250, which is above their whole per-slot traffic (Sepolia: ~56 attestations per slot over all subnets).

Above the 250 floor, the limiter admits at most 1.5 times the expected attestations per window, with the expected count taken when the window starts. Assuming 0.25 to 1 ms of CPU per accepted attestation (snappy decompression, SSZ decoding, committee lookup on the head state and batched BLS verification), the mainnet budgets correspond to about 0.05 to 0.2 cores for 2 subnets and 1.6 to 6.5 cores for all 64 subnets. As before, a burst around a window boundary can use the budgets of both adjacent windows.

The budget is recomputed by the first message of each window: one read lock on the head state to read its active validator set (normally cached) and one read lock on the topic subscriptions, every 6 seconds at most. Other messages only do the existing counter check.

## Not changed here

- Persistent subnets: by default (without `--caplin.subscribe-all-topics`), the initial ENR advertises attestation subnets 0 and 1, but Caplin does not subscribe to them (attestation topics are registered with an expiry in the past), so a node without validator duties receives no attestation subnet traffic. This is a separate issue.
- Duty subnets of non-aggregators: the committee subscription subscribes to the duty subnet also when the validator is not an aggregator; the validator spec requires the subscription only for aggregators. Subscribing only for aggregators would drop the subnets that only non-aggregator duties need, so a validator node would receive less attestation traffic, and a lower S can also lower the budget.
- There is no metric for the reason a message was ignored. The in-memory gossip stats count ignores by topic name with the subnet suffix removed, so all attestation subnets share one bucket; they do not record the reason, and their periodic printer is disabled. A counter labelled by reason would show how often the budget is reached.
- With fewer committees per slot than subnets (fewer than 262,144 active validators with 32-slot epochs and the default target committee size), a subnet carries a whole committee in some slots and none in others, so the expected count per subnet is an average and a window can hold more than budgeted. The budget is never lower than the previous 250.
- The budget is still one budget for all peers and is used before decoding, so messages that turn out to be invalid still use it.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/network/registry/register.go`: compute the attestation budget per window from the expected traffic; `RegisterGossipServices` takes a function returning the active validator count; `withGlobalTimeBasedRateLimiter` takes a function for the limit (the blob sidecar limiter still uses 32).
- `cl/phase1/network/registry/tb_rate_limiter.go`: read the limit from the function when a window starts.
- `cl/phase1/network/gossip/gossip_manager.go`: `ExpectedAttestations`, the attestations expected on the subscribed subnets within a window.
- `cl/phase1/network/gossip/gossip_subscription.go`: count the distinct attestation subnets that are actually subscribed.
- `cl/beacon/synced_data/synced_data.go`: `ActiveValidatorCount`, the active validators of the head state's epoch, 0 without a head state.
- `cmd/caplin/caplin1/run.go`: pass `syncedDataManager.ActiveValidatorCount`.
- Tests: `register_attestation_budget_test.go` and `tb_rate_limiter_test.go` (new), `active_validator_count_test.go` (new), `gossip_subscription_test.go`, and the new argument in `register_gloas_boundary_test.go`.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestAttestationGossipBudgetScalesWithExpectedTraffic` registers the services through `RegisterGossipServices`, subscribes 2 attestation subnets and publishes locally while the mocked `P2PManager.Host()` returns nil, so the self-publish bypass is off and every message runs through the validator. Rows: the mainnet config with 262,144 active validators and the Gnosis config with 65,536 (both expect 256 attestations per window, budget 384), and no head state (budget 250). Each row checks that a burst of the expected count (or 250 without a head state) reaches decoding, and that of budget + 100 messages exactly the budget does. On `main` (the test adapted to the old `RegisterGossipServices` signature) the mainnet and Gnosis rows fail: 250 of 256 messages reach decoding. With B forced to 1, the Gnosis row fails the same way.
- `TestSubscribedAttestationSubnetCount` (a subnet subscribed under two fork digests counts once, a joined but unsubscribed subnet and a sync committee topic do not count), `TestActiveValidatorCount` (0 without a head state, a validator that is not active yet does not count) and `TestTimeBasedRateLimiterRefreshesLimitEachWindow` (the limit is read once per window and follows the function across windows) fail when the count includes unsubscribed topics or counts topics instead of subnets, counts all validators, or reads the limit only once.
- `go test -p 2 -count=1 ./cl/phase1/network/registry/ ./cl/phase1/network/gossip/ ./cl/beacon/synced_data/ ./cmd/caplin/caplin1/` and `-race` on the first three packages passed.
- `make lint` reported 0 issues on two runs.
- `make erigon integration` succeeded.
author: domiwei

title: cl/phase1/network/registry: let one peer forward a whole PTC's votes at once
body:
Fixes #24972.

The `payload_attestation_message` topic allowed 8 messages per second per peer, with a burst of 16. PTC votes are due at the same point in the slot, so peers forward them in bursts. Gossipsub marks a message as seen before Caplin validates it, so a vote the limiter ignored was also dropped when other peers sent it, and the node lost it.

This change allows one peer to forward a whole committee's votes in one burst (`MaxPtcSize`), refilled at the same rate per second. The other topics' limits are unchanged.

Measured on a Sepolia node, 1 s into the next slot, over about 20 slots each:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| votes in the node's pool (of 512) | 455 | 511 |
| votes included by the next block | 510 | 512 |
author: lystopad

title: cl/beacon/handler: use the head root as the dependent root for slots after the head
body:
## Problem

`getDependentRoot` returns the head root only when the dependent slot equals the head slot. For a later dependent slot within the accepted lookahead, `GetBlockRootAtSlot` rejects every slot at or after the head state slot, so the backward scan reaches `headSlot - 1` and returns the root of the block before the head. If the head is the genesis block, it returns not found instead.

The Beacon API defines the dependent root as `get_block_root_at_slot(state, compute_start_slot_at_epoch(epoch - 1) - 1)` for attester duties and proposer duties v2, and as `get_block_root_at_slot(state, compute_start_slot_at_epoch(epoch) - 1)` for proposer duties v1, and both use the genesis block root on underflow.
