title: cl/beacon/handler: fix pending parent retry test flake
body:
When the completion observer runs late, the pending-parent retry worker can poll again after applying the envelope. The test mock counted that no-op poll as a third attempt, failing the exact count assertion in [Windows CI for #25471](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/actions/runs/40674305817/job/122769883364).

Make the mock return no work after application, matching `RetryPendingExecutionPayloadEnvelope`. Count actual attempts and explicitly assert that the envelope was applied. This is a test-only fix.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/beacon/handler: fix flaky timing in wait tests
body:
Fix flaky tests in `cl/beacon/handler`.

Two tests failed on the Windows serial runner in the merge queue (run https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/actions/runs/40759087718), one in each attempt of `make test-all`:

- `TestAwaitPendingParentPayloadDoesNotWaitForASlotThatIsNotCurrent`: `"142.2025ms" is not less than "100ms"`
- `TestGetEthV1ValidatorAttestationDataWaitsForSlotImport/request_canceled`: expected 500, got 200. The 60ms import-wait cap expired before the 20ms context cancel was observed.

Both assert wall-clock bounds only a few tens of milliseconds away from the events they measure, so a scheduling delay on a loaded runner crosses them.

## Changes

- `TestGetEthV1ValidatorAttestationDataWaitsForSlotImport`: the import-wait cap goes from 60ms to 1s, and the elapsed time is bounded by half of it (500ms) instead of a per-row 100ms `maxWait`. The 20ms cancel and import events stay the same, so the test still checks that the response comes from them and not from the cap.
- `pending_parent_wait_test.go`: the five "does not wait" bounds go from 100ms to 500ms. A broken wait in the not-current-slot tests takes 1.5s (the cutoff), so 500ms keeps a 3x margin.

## Verification

- Reproduced the failures locally by pinning the tests to one core at low priority next to CPU burners: 3 failures in 5 iterations before the change, 0 in 8 after.
- Mutation check: removing the `ctx.Done()` case in `waitForAttestationHead`, or the `IsSlotCurrentSlotWithMaximumClockDisparity` checks in `awaitPendingParentPayload` / `awaitHeadStateAfterChange`, still makes the affected tests fail.
- `go test ./cl/beacon/handler` passes, `make lint` is clean.

No new test is added: the change only widens the bounds of existing tests, and the reproduction used a stress harness rather than a new test.
author: lupin012

title: cl/das: skip cell proof verification for columns built from EL blobs
body:
Part of #25446.

The Fulu p2p spec says clients SHOULD skip verification of blobs retrieved from the local EL ("Distributed blob publishing using blobs retrieved from local execution-layer client"). The EL verifies cell proofs when it admits a blob transaction (Erigon's txpool does so in `validateTx` after Osaka), and Lighthouse, Prysm, Teku, Lodestar and Nimbus do not re-verify these columns. `ImportColumnsFromBlobs` verified all 128 × N cell proofs although it stores only the custody columns. It now keeps the structural checks (every blob, blob size, 128 proofs per blob, proof size), runs them before computing cells, and no longer verifies the proofs.

On a mainnet node, the time from the fleet's first sight of a block to its import there grew by ~28 ms per blob (0.06 s with no blobs, 0.58 s with 18–21). `BenchmarkImportColumnsFromBlobs` (new): 6 blobs 65.3 → 16.8 ms, 21 blobs 218 → 58 ms.

Tests: `TestImportColumnsFromBlobsTrustsELCellProofs` (fails before the change); the rejection cases keep the structural checks. `go test -race ./cl/das ./cl/phase1/network/services`, `make lint` (twice) and `make erigon integration` pass.
author: lystopad

title: cl/das: compute the cells of EL blobs in parallel
body:
Part of #25446.

`ImportColumnsFromBlobs` computed the cells of each blob one after another, and go-eth-kzg's `ComputeCells` does no internal parallelism (it ignores `numGoRoutines`). The new `peerdasutils.ComputeBlobsCells` computes them in parallel with `errgroup`, limited per call to `GOMAXPROCS` workers. It does not take the `rowRecoverySlots` of `RecoverMatrix`, so a head block's import never waits behind recovery rows; the trade-off is that an import and a recovery together can run about twice `GOMAXPROCS` workers, more with concurrent imports. `ComputeCells` moves from `cl/das` to `cl/das/utils` unchanged, and its callers in `cl/beacon/handler` use it from there. Prysm, Teku and Grandine also compute EL blob cells per blob in parallel.

`BenchmarkImportColumnsFromBlobs` (sequential → parallel): 6 blobs 17.0 → 3.6 ms, 21 blobs 58.8 → 8.2 ms on 16 cores; with `-cpu 4`, 3.6 and 10.7 ms.

Tests: `TestComputeBlobsCellsMatchesPerBlobCells`, `TestComputeBlobsCellsFailsOnInvalidBlob` and `TestComputeBlobsCellsDoesNotWaitForRecoverySlots` (new); `go test -race ./cl/das ./cl/das/utils`, `go test ./cl/beacon/handler`, `make lint` (twice) and `make erigon integration` pass.
author: lystopad

title: cl/das, cl/phase1/network/services: publish columns built from EL blobs and check the blob limit first
body:
Closes #25478. Part of #25446. Addresses domiwei's review of the release/3.8 backport #25474; the fixes land on main first and will be added to that backport.

The EL blob-to-column path from #25447 had two gaps:

1. **Blob limit.** A block queued on an unknown parent can start the EL import before gossip validation checked its commitment count. `importColumnsFromELBlobs` now returns before the EL call when the block has more commitments than `GetBlobParameters(epoch).MaxBlobsPerBlock`, which covers every trigger.
2. **Gossip behaviour** (Fulu p2p, "Distributed blob publishing using blobs retrieved from local execution-layer client": clients MUST behave as if the sidecar had been received via gossip). `ImportColumnsFromBlobs` stores the custody columns (all columns in archive mode) and returns the sidecars on the subnets the node subscribes to: the stored ones, or every built column with `--caplin.subscribe-all-topics`. The block service hands them to the new `DataColumnSidecarService.PublishColumnsFromEL`, with a context that does not expire with the EL wait. It marks each one in the anti-equivocation cache and publishes it on its subnet, unless a sidecar for its (slot, proposer, index) was already seen; a column whose publish fails is unmarked again, so a copy from gossip is still processed and relayed. Before marking or publishing, it applies the gossip finality rules (slot after the finalized epoch start, finalized checkpoint an ancestor of the block), since a queued block may have waited while finality moved on, and it publishes on the fork digest of the sidecar's epoch.

Also from the review: `TryScheduleRecover` now runs after every EL import (it returns early unless the node is in archive mode or is a supernode), so a non-archive supernode also recovers blobs; and `ProcessMessage`'s trigger is covered by a test.

`NewDataColumnSidecarService` takes the gossip manager, and `NewBlockService` takes the column service.

Tests (all fail with the corresponding change removed): `TestImportColumnsFromELBlobsSkipsBlockAboveBlobLimit`, `TestImportColumnsFromELBlobsPublishesStoredColumns`, `TestImportColumnsFromELBlobsDoesNotPublishFailedImport`, `TestPublishColumnsFromELPublishesUnseenColumnsAndMarksThemSeen`, `TestProcessMessageStartsELColumnsImportForValidGossipBlock` / `...DoesNotStart...ForInvalidGossipBlock`, `TestImportColumnsFromBlobsSupernodeSchedulesRecovery`, `TestPublishColumnsFromELSkipsColumnsFinalityNoLongerAllows`, `TestImportColumnsFromBlobsPublishesAllColumnsWhenSubscribedToAllTopics`, `TestImportColumnsFromELBlobsUsesTheBlobLimitOfTheBlockEpoch`, `TestImportColumnsFromELBlobsPublishesAfterTheImportContextExpires`, `TestPublishColumnsFromELReleasesTheClaimOfAFailedPublish`. `go test -race ./cl/das/... ./cl/phase1/network/services ./cmd/caplin/...`, `make lint` (twice) and `make erigon integration` pass.

#25510 and #25514 touch `cl/das/el_blobs.go` too (verification and cell computation, not storage or publishing); whichever merges later needs a small rebase there.

Follow-up: #25583 (the gossip path ignores valid non-custody sidecars on subscribed subnets instead of relaying them).
author: lystopad

title: cl/beacon: cover production error priority and cancellation
body:
Follow-up to #23393. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

- Pin the first-error-wins rule when payload polling sees failures with equal priority.
- Verify that fork-choice cancellation after request cancellation logs at Debug without an internal-cancellation marker.
- Verify that an internal cancellation observed while the request is active still logs at Error after the request is canceled.
- Rename the diagnostic ranking type to `productionErrorPriority`.
- Correct test comments about caller cancellation. Node shutdown can leave HTTP requests active during the API drain, so it is not equivalent to caller cancellation.
author: yperbasis

title: cl: enforce peer bans for invalid backfill envelopes
body:
A peer serving invalid Gloas envelopes can repeatedly stall historical backfill. Backfill now validates envelopes against their canonical blocks during fetching, while the serving peer is still known. This includes signature checks when the signer's public key is known. When envelope validation or RPC parsing detects invalid data, backfill bans the serving peer and retries missing envelopes within the batch deadline. HTTP fallback validates only newly fetched envelopes.

A dedicated Sentinel ban RPC bypasses the 32-peer grace threshold for invalid data. Both by-root and by-range backfill requests use it. Regression tests cover bid mismatches, forged signatures, malformed RPC responses, recovery through an honest peer, and actual disconnection with only one peer.

The decoder and helper refactors, along with comment-only edits, rely on existing tests (TDD exemption).

Partially addresses https://github.com/ethereum-bounty/erigon/issues/57. The history-stage restart loop when no source has the required envelope remains tracked in https://github.com/erigontech/security/issues/86.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/phase1/execution_client: reject RLP-wrapped typed transactions
body:
Caplin accepted RLP-wrapped typed transactions through direct payload validation and forward-sync block collection, while the Engine API rejected the same encoding. Apply the existing guard before decoding payload transactions in both paths so wrapped transactions cannot reach execution insertion.

Fixes https://github.com/ethereum-bounty/erigon/issues/58.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/beacon/handler: check blob data on the legacy envelope POST route
body:
## Summary

`POST /eth/v1/beacon/execution_payload_envelope` (the legacy route) called fork choice `OnExecutionPayload` with `checkBlobData=false`. The canonical `POST /eth/v1/beacon/execution_payload_envelopes` route and the gossip path both pass `true`. So the legacy route could import and persist an envelope, which makes the FULL variant of its block available in fork choice, without the data-availability check that Gloas `on_execution_payload` requires.

Changes:

- `processExecutionPayloadEnvelope` always calls `OnExecutionPayload` with `checkBlobData=true`. Its `checkBlobData` parameter is removed, because the function has one caller.
- The legacy route now also attaches the cached blob data of a local non-self-build bid (`pendingLocalExecutionPayloadEnvelopeContents`), as the canonical route does when `Eth-Blob-Data-Included: false`. Without this, now that the check is on, an envelope for such a bid that is posted on the legacy route could stay queued until its columns become available through another path.

## Behaviour change

When the columns of an envelope are not available, the legacy route now answers 400, as the canonical route does with `Eth-Blob-Data-Included: false` (beacon-APIs `envelope_post.yaml` prescribes 400 for an envelope without blob data when the node has none cached). Fork choice still queues the envelope, and it schedules deferred column sync when PeerDAS is configured and the node is not syncing. The envelope is not published on gossip. The handler releases the `(block root, builder index)` admission key without marking it as seen, so a re-POST is admitted again, unless the background retry has already imported the envelope. Before, the legacy route skipped the check and returned 200.

## Tests

`TestPostExecutionPayloadEnvelopeAttachesPendingLocalBlobData` now runs for both handler variants, and it also asserts that fork choice is called with `checkBlobData=true`. With the old production code, the new `legacy` subtest fails with 202 and no stored columns. If only the `checkBlobData` change is reverted to the old route-dependent value, the `legacy` subtest fails on the `checkBlobData` assertion.

`TestPostExecutionPayloadEnvelopesRejectsStatefulEnvelopeWhenColumnsAreMissing` now runs on both routes. Its fixture gave the envelope a different builder index than the bid, so its 400 came from the builder-index check and not from the missing-columns branch; the bid now uses the envelope's builder index. Each subtest asserts 400 with no event and no gossip publish, then 200 and one publish on a re-POST after the columns become available. With the `canonical` condition still on the 400 case, the legacy subtest fails because the first POST returns 202; if that first assertion is removed, the re-POST fails with 400 "already seen". Without the 400 case, both subtests fail with 202.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

No beacon-APIs release defines the singular `POST /eth/v1/beacon/execution_payload_envelope`. Deleting the legacy route and its `canonical` flag would remove the remaining differences between the two routes.
author: domiwei

title: cl: harden block persistence and head publication
body:
Follow-up to domiwei's review of #25442. A block accepted before its index write completes could delay head publication until the next slot. During a storage outage, each queued job also retried the same failing database.

- [Head publication](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/pull/25442#discussion_r4410728323): treat missing indices as an expected wait and log at Debug. Block-index commits from sync, gossip, and API publishing wake publication, with a one-second fallback before and after Gloas. The fork-choice stage waits for the required indices before updating the canonical chain and served head.
- [Storage retries](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/pull/25442#discussion_r4410728328): share storage backoff across scheduled jobs. A storage failure delays further attempts for scheduled jobs; the current scan still checks remaining jobs for expiry. Jobs without an accepted block can expire; accepted blocks remain queued and are persisted after recovery.
- [Signed copies](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/pull/25442#discussion_r4410728334): sync persists the signed copy retained by fork choice. A peer's copy of a known block cannot overwrite its validated signature, and failed writes keep their execution-insertion work.
- [Peer scoring](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/pull/25442#discussion_r4410728341): classify a failed accepted-block write as a local error so forward sync does not ban the serving peer.

The [acceptance contract](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/pull/25442#discussion_r4410728345) is documented once on the fork-choice interface. Regression tests reproduced the behavior failures before the fixes; refactors and comment cleanup use existing coverage.

Broader persistence and head-publication ownership, including retained-block memory limits, is tracked in #25544. The ignored-publication case remains in #25483.
author: yperbasis

title: cl/phase1/forkchoice/fork_graph: skip re-dumping an already dumped head state
body:
## Problem

On Gloas the ForkChoice stage runs again for the same head root when the head's payload status changes from EMPTY to FULL (`GetExecutionHead` changes and `sleep_for_slot.go` wakes the stage), and again about once per second while the forkchoice update returns busy. Each run calls `postForkchoiceOperations`, which dumps the head state with `DumpBeaconStateOnDisk`. The envelope does not change the beacon state, so every extra run encodes and rewrites the same state for the same root.

A head-state dump takes about 405 ms p50 on a mainnet node with the current dump code (no fsync since #25251), and it holds `stateDumpLock`, which disk state reads (replays) also need. By code reasoning this can add up to 8 redundant dumps per epoch on Gloas (one per dump slot, more while the forkchoice update is busy). There is no Gloas mainnet data for this yet.

## Fix

`forkGraphDisk` remembers the block root and slot of its last successful state dump, guarded by `stateDumpLock`. `DumpBeaconStateOnDisk` returns early when both match. The slot is part of the key because a state advanced through empty slots keeps its block root but has different content. The marker is cleared before each write and set only after the write finished and the file closed without error, so a failed or panicked write is retried (stage panics are recovered, so the next run would otherwise skip a truncated file).

## Tests

New tests in `fork_graph_test.go` count state-file writes through the existing failing-fs wrapper:
- the same root and slot dumped twice writes once (red on main: 2 writes);
- a close error is retried (`TestDumpBeaconStateReturnsCloseError`);
- a panic during the write is retried (`TestDumpBeaconStateRetriesAfterPanic`);
- a different root is still written;
- the same root at a different slot is still written, and the file holds the later state;
- a failed later-slot write does not block a new dump of the earlier slot.

Each test fails when the production branch it targets is removed.

## Out of scope

- `stateDumpLock` contention between state dumps and replays in general, and making the state dump atomic (temp file + rename).
- Avoiding the repeated ForkChoice stage run itself.

Related to #25120 and #25136.
author: domiwei

title: cl/utils/bls: aggregate public keys with blst batch addition
body:
## Problem

`Signature.VerifyAggregate` used blst `FastAggregateVerify`. It sums the public keys with `P1Aggregate.Aggregate`, which starts GOMAXPROCS goroutines and makes one cgo call plus one `runtime.Gosched` per key. On mainnet, each Electra block carries aggregates with about 25-30k keys in total, and they are verified inside the block state transition under the fork-choice lock. With 32k keys the key aggregation alone takes about 13-16 ms on an M3 Pro, and more when the cores are busy.

## Change

- Sum the keys with blst batch addition (`P1Affines.Add`, which calls `blst_p1s_add`), then verify once against the aggregate key. The flags are the same as inside `FastAggregateVerify`: the signature is group-checked, the keys are not validated again (they were validated when decoded). An empty key list and a nil key still return false.
- At most 512 keys go into one cgo call. The chunks are summed on up to GOMAXPROCS goroutines, each with its own buffer, and the partial sums are added in Go.

Why 512: `blst_p1s_add` puts its scratch buffer on the C stack (`alloca` of `min(n, 1024)` points at 144 bytes each, so up to `SCRATCH_LIMIT` = 144 KiB), see supranational/blst#142. Go starts cgo threads with the libc default thread stack size, which is 128 KiB on musl. 512 points need 72 KiB of scratch. A compile-time check keeps the chunk scratch below the musl thread stack.

Which builds are affected: glibc builds (8 MiB thread stacks) are not. Of our images, only `debug.Dockerfile` (Alpine) is musl. The root `Dockerfile` is Debian, CI builds the Hive image from it, hive's own erigon Dockerfiles are Debian too, and hive runs erigon with `--externalcl`. On musl, passing all keys to one `P1Affines.Add` call crashes with SIGBUS at 2048 keys under GOMAXPROCS=1. With more procs, blst splits the call into at most GOMAXPROCS slices of at least 512 points, so 32768 keys still give slices of more than 1024 points (the full 144 KiB of scratch) with fewer than 32 procs.

Callers that benefit: block attestation verification, attester slashings (gossip, block, Beacon API pool), and the sync aggregate (512 keys or fewer, so one call without goroutines). Gossip aggregates and sync committee contributions use `AggregatePublickKeys` with `VerifyMultipleSignatures` and are not changed.

## Results

`BenchmarkSignatureVerifyAggregate`, 32768 keys, Apple M3 Pro:

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| GOMAXPROCS unset (12) | 15.8 ms | 1.8 ms |
| GOMAXPROCS=4 | 11.4 ms | 2.5 ms |

Each worker allocates one buffer of up to 512 keys (48 KiB), so a 32768-key call allocates about 200 KB with 4 workers and about 600 KB with 12.

The same benchmark on the machine of the mainnet dev node (Intel Xeon E-2288G, 16 threads), run with `nice -n 19` next to the running node. The old and new test binaries ran alternately, six times each; the table shows the median:

| Keys | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.77 ms | 0.77 ms |
| 128 | 0.90 ms | 0.79 ms |
| 513 | 1.10 ms | 0.92 ms |
| 2048 | 1.65 ms | 1.15 ms |
| 32768 | 12.5 ms | 2.6 ms |

For 2048 and 32768 keys the ranges of the six runs do not overlap. With 16 workers, a 32768-key call allocates about 800 KB.

Mainnet dev node: block attestation verification takes 9 ms at p50 and 11 ms at p90, for 25.4k keys per block at p50. That run had no baseline with the old code; the benchmark above is the same-machine comparison. The fork-choice lock hold after `newPayload` went from 50 to 44 ms at p50 compared to the previous day, which is within day-to-day noise, so I do not claim more than about 10 ms per block from the node data.

## Tests

- The aggregate verification gives the same results for 1 key and for 511, 512, 513, 1024, 1025 and 4096 keys; a wrong message, a missing key, an extra key and a nil key return false; empty key lists keep the existing behaviour.
- With 16 or more keys (blst's batch path): an adjacent duplicate pair that reaches the doubling branch (18 keys), an adjacent P/-P pair, a P/-P pair in a 32-key batch whose infinity result goes into the next tree round, and a cancelling pair across a 512-key chunk boundary.
- With GOMAXPROCS=2, so that one worker sums several chunks (1025 and 2049 keys).
- Benchmarks for `bls.VerifyAggregate` (with the key cache warm) and `Signature.VerifyAggregate`. The tests and benchmarks share one lazily built set of keys, and the 32768-key benchmark size runs only outside `-short`, so `make test-bench` does not sign 32768 keys.

These tests pass on `main` as well, because the change does not alter results. The musl stack limit has no test in the repository, because it needs a thread with a small stack. I checked it with a cgo probe that calls `Signature.VerifyAggregate` from a pthread with a 128 KiB stack and GOMAXPROCS=1: a version that passes all keys to one `P1Affines.Add` call crashes with SIGBUS at 2048 keys, while `main` and this PR pass at 1024, 2048 and 8192 keys. I did not run it on a real Alpine host or inside `debug.Dockerfile`.

title: cl/phase1/stages: serve a validated head while the execution layer applies it
body:
## Problem

The fork choice stage (`doForkchoiceRoutine`) sends `engine.ForkChoiceUpdate` and waits for it. Only after that does it:
- update the canonical chain;
- emit the head event and produce the attestation data;
- publish the head to `syncedData`, which `GET /eth/v1/beacon/blocks/head/root` and the other `head` endpoints read.

Every head therefore reaches validators later by the duration of the execution layer's head commit. On a mainnet node we measured 0.23 s at the median and 0.35 s at p90 between the block event and the head event.

The delay matters most for blocks that arrive late in the slot. A sync committee message is due at 4 s. For a block first seen by the network at about 3.3–3.6 s, the delay moves our head past that point, so the validator signs the previous block and the vote is not included. Over a sync period on that node, the missed votes concentrated on exactly those blocks.

## Change

- `computeAndNotifyServicesOfNewForkChoice` is split into `selectForkChoiceHead` and `notifyServicesOfHead`. The combined function is kept for its existing callers.
- For a pre-Gloas head whose payload has a recorded VALID verdict from `newPayload` (`GetRecentExecutionPayloadStatusByRoot`), `doForkchoiceRoutine` runs `notifyServicesOfHead` (the forkchoice update and the RPC status) concurrently with the canonical chain update and the post-forkchoice operations. It waits for the update before it commits and always before it returns, so the next stage never runs while the update is in flight.
- The payload of such a head was validated by `newPayload` on import, so the update only moves the execution head. Lighthouse orders it the same way: it switches its cached head and emits the head events first, and spawns the execution layer update afterwards.
- Any other head keeps the current order, where the update comes first: a forward-synced head that skipped `newPayload`, an optimistic or invalidated one, one whose verdict is no longer cached, and a Gloas head. For such a head the update is the first execution check, and a rejection stops it before it is served.
- While block indices are still pending (the early return added in #25533), the routine returns the update's error instead of dropping it.
- If the update fails after the head was published, the stage commits the canonical chain, so the database matches the head the API serves, and then returns the error. Before, a failed update left both unchanged. The timeout and busy cases are unchanged.

## Tests

The tests were written first. On `main`:
- `TestForkchoiceRoutinePublishesValidatedHeadWhileExecutionAppliesIt` fails: the forkchoice update blocks, and the head is published only after it returns.
- `TestForkchoiceRoutineReturnsExecutionErrorAfterPublishingValidatedHead` fails: the head is never published, and the canonical chain is not written.

`TestForkchoiceRoutineWaitsForExecutionOnHeadWithoutValidation` pins the forward-synced case: no publication while the update is in flight, publication after it returns. The predicate is pinned by `TestPublishHeadBeforeExecutionOnlyForValidatedPreGloasHeads`, which covers validated, optimistic, invalidated, no-verdict and Gloas heads.

Mutation checks:
- Accepting a head without a VALID verdict fails the predicate test and the forward-synced routine test.
- Dropping the Gloas check fails the predicate test.
- Never publishing early fails both routine tests.

Run locally:
- `go test -race ./cl/phase1/stages/` passes.
- `make lint` is clean on two runs.
- `make erigon integration` builds.

## Not in this PR

- Gloas heads. Their payload may still be unverified when the update is sent, so they keep the current order.
author: lystopad

title: cl/phase1/network/services: relay valid Fulu data column sidecars outside custody
body:
Part of #25583. Builds on #25522 (merged).

## Problem

`processFuluMessage` returned `ErrIgnore` for a sidecar whose column is not in the node's custody, before any validation. The node only gets such sidecars on subnets it subscribes to beyond its custody, which today means `--caplin.subscribe-all-topics`. An IGNORE verdict is not forwarded, so on those subnets the node received valid sidecars but never relayed them.

The Fulu `data_column_sidecar_{subnet_id}` gossip conditions have no custody condition. A sidecar that passes them should be accepted and forwarded.

## Change

In normal custody mode, a non-custody sidecar now goes through the same validation as a custody one:
- If it is valid, the tuple is claimed in the seen cache and the sidecar is accepted, so it is forwarded.
- It is not stored, and no blob recovery is scheduled.
- An invalid one is now rejected instead of ignored.

Custody sidecars are processed as before. The cost: a node subscribed to every column subnet now verifies the KZG proofs of every column it relays, which a node that forwards those columns has to do anyway.

## Not in this PR (tracked in #25583)

- **Archive mode** still ignores sidecars once more than half of a block's columns are stored or its blobs are recovered. The spec-consistent fix there is to publish the recovered columns and mark them seen, after which later copies are ignored as duplicates. That is a separate change.
- **Gloas** has the same custody check. There, a non-custody sidecar for a block that is not yet known would also enter the deferred queue, so it needs its own change.

## Tests

The tests were written first; both fail on the base branch:
- `TestProcessMessage_WhenValidSidecarOutsideCustody_AcceptsWithoutStoring`: the sidecar is accepted and its tuple marked seen, with no storage write and no recovery scheduled (strict mocks). If storage is not skipped for a non-custody column, the test fails on an unexpected `WriteColumnSidecars` call.
- `TestProcessMessage_WhenInvalidSidecarOutsideCustody_ReturnsError`: with failing KZG proofs, the result is a REJECT error, not `ErrIgnore`.

Run locally:
- `go test -race ./cl/phase1/network/services/` passes.
- `make lint` is clean on two runs.
- `make erigon integration` builds.
author: lystopad

title: cl/phase1/network/registry: let one peer forward a slot of each sync subnet at once
body:
Fixes #25592.

The `sync_committee_{subnet_id}` topics allowed 8 messages per second per peer, burst 16, in one bucket shared by all sync subnets. A subnet carries 128 messages per slot, signed at the same point in the slot, so a mesh peer forwards most of them in one burst. Gossipsub marks a message as seen before Caplin validates it, so a message the limiter ignored was also dropped when other peers sent it: the node neither pooled nor relayed it. On an instrumented lab node the limiter ignored about 69% of the sync messages that reached Caplin, and every sync-message IGNORE came from it.

## Change

The limit stays per peer, but is keyed by peer and topic and sized from the config:
- the burst is one slot of one subnet, `SyncCommitteeSize / SyncCommitteeSubnetCount` (128 on mainnet, Hoodi and Gnosis; 8 on minimal);
- it refills over `SecondsPerSlot`.

An honest peer can relay a whole subnet in one burst, and a peer that floods one subnet is still capped at one slot's worth there. The other topics' limits are unchanged, including sync contributions, whose IGNOREs in the lab came from validation, not the limiter.

For comparison, Lighthouse has no per-peer count limit on gossip; it bounds global work queues (2,048 sync messages). Prysm has no per-peer limit on sync committee messages.

## Tests

`TestSyncCommitteeMessageRateLimiterAdmitsEachSubnetsSlotFromOnePeer` covers the mainnet and minimal presets. One peer sends a full slot on every subnet, which is admitted, and then one more message on a full subnet, which is refused. On the old limit it fails at message 17 on mainnet, and on minimal at the third subnet, because the bucket was shared.

`go test -race ./cl/phase1/network/registry` passes, `make lint` is clean twice, and `make erigon integration` builds.

A lab A/B with the limiter relaxed is running; its results will follow in a comment.

title: cl/phase1/network/services: verify sync committee messages before accepting them
body:
Fixes #25604. Follow-up to the #25593 review (domiwei).

## Problem

On the gossip path, `syncCommitteeMessagesService.ProcessMessage` queued the BLS check with `AsyncVerifySyncCommitteeMessage` and returned nil, so libp2p accepted, and could forward, a sync committee message before its signature was verified. #24629 fixed this for attestations, aggregates, voluntary exits and BLS-to-execution changes. The queue send also ran while the service mutex and the `SyncedDataManager` read lock were held, so a full queue stalled every sync message and, with a head-state write pending, every new head-state reader. #25593 raised the per-peer budget on these topics, which made this path easier to fill.

## Change

- `checkMessage` runs the checks that need no signature and builds the verification data under the service mutex and the head-state read lock, as before.
- `ProcessMessage` then releases the locks and waits for this message's own verdict through the new `BatchSignatureVerifier.VerifySyncCommitteeMessage` (the same `verifyAndWait` as the other topics):
  - a valid signature returns nil, so the message is accepted;
  - an invalid one returns `ErrInvalidBlsSignature`, so it is rejected instead of forwarded;
  - a cancelled wait returns `ErrIgnore`.
- Batching is kept: concurrent validators share a batch.
- After a valid verdict, `storeVerifiedMessage` takes the service mutex again, records the message as the one valid message for its (subnet, slot, validator) and adds it to the pool. If a different message for that key was verified at the same time and recorded first, this one returns `ErrIgnore`, so verification runs without the lock and the first-valid-message rule still holds. This covers the REST path (`ImmediateVerification`) too, which used to run its callback under the lock.
- A duplicate of an already verified, not yet published message still returns nil without verification.

Sync contributions have the same accept-before-verify path and are left for a separate change (noted in #25604).

The second commit shortens the comment on the sync limiter from #25593: the seen-cache rationale was spelled out on three limiters (review nit).

The third commit addresses the Copilot finding: the first version stored the seen entry in the verification callback, after the lock was released, so two different valid messages for one key verified at the same time were both accepted.

## Tests

- `TestSyncCommitteesGossipRejectsInvalidSignatureBeforeAccepting`: a gossip message whose signature fails verification. It failed on `main`, where `ProcessMessage` returned nil, and now returns `ErrInvalidBlsSignature`.
- `TestSyncCommitteesGossipWaitsForVerificationWithoutHoldingLocks`: while a gossip message waits for its verdict, a head-state publication completes. It pins that the wait holds no lock; it passes on `main` too, where nothing waits.
- `TestSyncCommitteesAcceptsOneOfConcurrentlyVerifiedMessagesForTheSameValidator`: two different valid messages for one validator and slot are verified at the same time; exactly one is accepted and the other is ignored. It failed on the first version of this PR, where both were accepted.

`go test -race ./cl/phase1/network/services ./cl/beacon/handler` passes, `make lint` is clean twice, and `make erigon integration` builds.

title: cl/beacon/builder: fix admission test maximum counter
body:
Fix the flaky maximum counter in `TestDynamicBuilderCallsShareBoundedAdmission` ([failed CI job](https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/actions/runs/41312972395/job/124867095186)). The comparison and CAS used separate loads, allowing a request with count 23 to overwrite a recorded maximum of 24. Each CAS attempt now uses one captured value.

Confirmed with a controlled interleaving: 24 active calls left the old counter at 23; the fixed loop keeps 24. The existing test passed 4,000 race-enabled runs across 1, 2, 4 and 8 CPUs, and the full builder package passes with `-race`.
